blogs.title: Threats Aren’t Persecution: How Jimenez v. Bondi Tightens the Persecution Threshold
blogs.description: This post dissects the Tenth Circuit’s reasoning that a series of threats – even when accompanied by psychological distress – does not rise to the level of “persecution” under § 1101(a)(42)(A). By tracing the line from Karki v. Holder through Brandy v. Holder up to this decision, the article explains why the court demands more than intimidation – it seeks concrete physical injury or a sustained campaign of severe harm. The piece evaluates whether the cumulative‑effect approach articulated in Ritonga v. Holder can rescue threat‑only narratives and explores policy implications for future asylum seekers from violence‑prone regions who rely heavily on fear‑based evidence.

blogs.title: Political Opinion or Personal Grudge? The Central‑Reason Test in Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: Focusing on the nexus requirement, this entry unpacks how the court applied the “central reason” standard to reject a claim that persecution was motivated by political opinion. It contrasts the Tenth Circuit’s insistence that political motive must be more than peripheral with earlier cases like Dallakoti and Yuk, and discusses why non‑state actors—here a narco‑guerrilla leader—pose a doctrinal challenge for applicants asserting political persecution. The article also notes that petitioners failed to invoke a particular social group claim, leaving an unexamined avenue that could have altered the nexus analysis.

blogs.title: "Unable or Unwilling" Without a Police Report: Reporting Requirements After Jimenez
blogs.description: This commentary examines how Jimenez reinforces a strict evidentiary burden on asylum seekers to show that the government was unable or unwilling to protect them. By analyzing the court’s reliance on Aviles‑Gonzalez and its dismissal of vague claims of governmental complicity absent formal police filings, the piece highlights a procedural hurdle that many claimants cannot surmount when fearing retaliation for reporting. It offers practical guidance for counsel—when to argue futility versus danger in filing reports—and assesses whether this approach aligns with international refugee standards.

blogs.title: The Internal Relocation Paradox: Safe‑Relocation Standards After Jimenez
blogs.description: This article critiques the Tenth Circuit’s internal‑relocation analysis, which hinged on a brief three‑week stay with family in rural Bogotá as proof that petitioners could safely move within Colombia. The post reviews statutory guidance under 8 C.F.R.§ 1208.13(b)(1)(i), compares Tenth Circuit reasoning with other circuits that demand more substantial evidence of systemic risk, and questions whether temporary refuge is sufficient to defeat an internal‑relocation defense. It also considers how this narrow view may affect future cases involving applicants from countries where criminal groups wield quasi‑governmental power.
